video_title: Lindy Teammate: Flo Crivello on Multiplayer Agents, Memory & Why He'd Ban the Chinese Models He Uses
gist: Flo Crivello, founder and CEO of Lindy, launches Lindy Teammate — a Slack-resident multiplayer AI employee that crawls a company's entire Slack, wiki and meeting history into a git-backed, agent-maintained memory file system — and discloses unusually specific engineering and unit economics: an 85% prompt cache rate, negative gross margins on the new product, DeepSeek as the default main-driver model, an 8x error-rate drop from a self-improvement loop, and roughly $10,000 of automated prompt re-optimization per new frontier model release. He argues context now matters more than intelligence, that RAG loses to agent-managed file-system memory, that division of labor is a bad reason to build multi-agent systems, and that the current human-AI centaur phase is real but temporary. He closes with the contrarian position that Chinese frontier models — including the DeepSeek his own company runs on — should be banned in the US, while conceding an insurance-and-audit regime as a workable compromise.

themes.theme: Multiplayer AI employees as the next form factor

insights.claim: Lindy's new product, Lindy Teammate, is an AI employee that lives inside a company's Slack, connects to its tools and accumulates shared team context rather than per-user context — Crivello frames this multiplayer shift as the analog of moving from emailed document revisions to Google Docs.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Single-player chat assistants may be a transitional form factor; agent products without shared org memory and a home on the collaboration surface are exposed to Slack-native multiplayer entrants.
insights.quote: I compare the difference between multiplayer and single player AI as between like sending each other weird documents and Google Docs like an actual shared document.

insights.claim: Crivello argues that as AGI arrives, raw intelligence matters less and context matters more, illustrating with the claim that John von Neumann magically appearing at your office would be less useful over the next hour than a random coworker who already has the context.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Defensibility in the agent layer shifts from model access to accumulated proprietary org context — a moat argument favoring context-hoarding application companies over thin model wrappers.
insights.quote: as we now arguably have AGI, intelligence actually matters less and less comparatively speaking and context matters more and more

insights.claim: Lindy treats meetings as a first-class citizen of its memory system rather than relying on external notetakers, on the view that roughly 90% of the most up-to-date company knowledge lives in meetings and that every relationship, project and initiative has a meeting around it.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Standalone meeting-recording tools risk commoditization as a feature inside memory-owning agent platforms; watch for consolidation pressure on that category.
insights.quote: I think like those multiplayer agentic systems cannot really get meetings to like granola or whatever like I think you have to really incorporate it in your system as a first class citizen

insights.claim: Lindy resolves the privacy problem of multiplayer memory with a two-tier design — a public workspace layer and a private personal layer — populated by a background memory agent that Crivello says runs roughly every 15 minutes rather than on a daily cycle.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Public/private tiering is the practical gating factor for enterprise adoption of org-wide agent memory; vendors without a credible answer stall in security review.
insights.quote: We call it napping not sleeping. So like it runs every something like 15 minutes like why why would you need to sleep every 24 hours?

insights.claim: Crivello predicts the next six months of AI product development will be defined by multiplayer AI and human-AI hybrid Iron Man suit products rather than single-user assistants, and expects that from more companies than just Lindy.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A near-dated, falsifiable roadmap call for the agent application layer — useful for timing bets on collaboration-surface-native agent startups.
insights.quote: I do believe the next six months are going to be about multiplayer AI and about this like Iron Man suit

insights.claim: Crivello is explicitly bearish on RAG as the primary memory approach and bullish on agent-managed text-and-file-system memory, because an agent with its own meta-memory understands what it is looking at and the memory stays inspectable and editable.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A negative signal for pure vector-DB and RAG-infrastructure businesses and a positive one for agent-native file-system and memory-orchestration vendors.
insights.quote: I think this is why I'm ultimately quite bearish on rag as an approach and I'm very bullish on on on this like agentic management approach because you have an actual agent which has its own memory

insights.claim: Lindy routes all memory access through a single memory agent even though other agents could read the file system directly, so it can log every query, answer and hop count and then have the agent restructure its own memory during downtime to minimize hops on frequently asked questions.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Query logs turn memory into a self-optimizing cache — a compounding advantage that accrues with usage and is hard for a new entrant to replicate cold.
insights.quote: it will it restructure its own memory to reduce the number of hops that is needed to retrieve like the most frequently asked questions

insights.claim: Lindy backs its agent file system with a git repository so that forked memory sub-agents working the same corpus can merge and rebase instead of colliding, which Crivello notes also yields version history for free.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Git as the concurrency primitive for multi-agent write conflicts is becoming a standard pattern — a tailwind for git-backed agent-infrastructure vendors.
insights.quote: the way human organizations have solved that is via git

insights.claim: Crivello believes memory ultimately belongs in the weights and calls the current file-system approach a hack, saying that with infinite resources he would train a LoRA per user — shifting the system from napping every 15 minutes to dreaming daily or weekly.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: If per-user LoRAs become viable, today's memory-orchestration layer gets absorbed into the model layer — an obsolescence risk for memory-infrastructure investments.
insights.quote: It does feel like memory belongs to the weights. This does feel like a little bit of a hack.

insights.claim: Crivello predicts LoRA-based per-user memory arrives within roughly six months and that a frontier lab may ship it first, with inference-time swapping of LoRAs rather than storage being the hard engineering problem.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A dated call to test: if labs ship per-user weight personalization, application-layer memory moats compress fast.
insights.quote: I think the Laura thing is going to happen soon in the next six months. I think even like one of the frontier labs may do it.

themes.theme: Context-bucket trees and agent caching economics

insights.claim: Lindy's core context-scaling technique is context buckets — when an action or MCP call returns too much data, it is exposed to the agent as a summary plus a sub-agent standing in for the full payload, which the agent can query and manipulate with Unix utilities under its own cache.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A concrete, copyable pattern for controlling agent token spend; Crivello explicitly invites replication, so treat it as table stakes rather than a moat.
insights.quote: I hope please you know like copy us like I will just we just don't have the time to publish

insights.claim: Because naive recursive context buckets create linear retrieval depth, Lindy built a self-balancing 100-ary tree — choosing red-black-style balancing over AVL because rebalancing regenerates context packets and destroys the cache — giving access to roughly 10,000 buckets of 200,000 tokens each, about two billion tokens, within two LLM calls.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Quantifies that effectively unbounded agent memory is already an engineering-solved problem at two hops, weakening the claim that model context-window length is the binding constraint.
insights.quote: you're literally no more than two LLM calls away from being able to access 10,000 context buckets, each one of which contains 200,000 tokens

insights.claim: Lindy runs an 85% prompt cache rate, considers that lower than it should be, and alerts on it because any system change can drop it to 65% — a gap Crivello says is worth almost 2x on price.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Cache-rate management, not model choice, is the dominant near-term lever on agent gross margin — a diligence question to ask any agent startup.
insights.quote: Our current cache rate is at 85%.

insights.claim: Because a cache hit is roughly 10x cheaper, Crivello concludes you should almost never mix models inside a single agent — a cheaper model only wins if it is more than 10x cheaper, which DeepSeek Flash may not be once inferior third-party caching is accounted for.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Caching economics create real per-family switching friction and lock-in, partially offsetting the commoditization thesis for frontier model providers.
insights.quote: We have found you should almost never use multiple models powering the same agent.

insights.claim: Onboarding a 20-person team with years of Slack history consumes only about 3 to 5 million tokens of initial hydration, and Crivello says the bottleneck is Slack's API rate limits rather than the LLM.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Upfront ingestion cost is far smaller than intuition suggests, so free-trial land-and-expand is affordable; the real friction is platform API policy, a dependency risk on Slack.
insights.quote: for a team of 20 that's going to tend to consume 5 million tokens at most you know 3 to 5 million tokens

themes.theme: Model mix: DeepSeek as the default driver

insights.claim: Lindy currently runs DeepSeek as its main driver model across the entire product by default — not merely for cheap sub-agent tasks — though customers can manually select Sonnet or Opus in settings, and Lindy is reconsidering the default because Lindy Teammate requires beefier compute.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A production agent company defaulting its whole stack to a Chinese open-weight model is direct evidence of revenue leakage from US frontier labs at the application layer.
insights.quote: Right now we're running on Deepseek. Deepse is the main driver.

insights.claim: Crivello characterizes DeepSeek Flash as roughly Claude Sonnet 4.6 level, slightly below, while being about 100x cheaper — so even losing 2x to inferior caching leaves it 50x cheaper, the difference between a $1,000 and a $50,000 bill.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Quantifies the price-performance gap driving open-weight substitution; frontier labs must close roughly a 50x effective cost gap or cede the volume tier.
insights.quote: if you look at like a deepseek flash, it's set 4.6 levelish, a bit less, but kind of is

insights.claim: Crivello estimates Chinese open models are three to six months behind US frontier models and describes the qualitative gap as spikiness — DeepSeek usually still finds a working answer but takes more turns, making it slower and more expensive than headline token prices imply.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Turn count, not per-token price, is the real cost metric for agentic workloads — a needed correction to naive model-substitution cost comparisons.
insights.quote: It's more spiky. It takes more turns very often to find something that works.

insights.claim: Lindy has returned to negative gross margins with Lindy Teammate after the earlier switch to a Chinese model had let it stop subsidizing, and Crivello says he accepts this because he deliberately builds for the next generation of models.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: AI-employee products are still sold below cost; revenue growth in this category should be discounted for subsidy, with margin recovery dependent on continued model price deflation.
insights.quote: with lindy teammate were back at it and back into frankly negative gross margin territory

insights.claim: Crivello states that AI employees still cost more than a human employee today, but expects that to stop being true very soon.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Defines the crossing point at which labor substitution becomes an economic default rather than an experiment — the key variable for displacement timing.
insights.quote: these things still cost more than the human employee but not for very long

insights.claim: Crivello reports that model families have not converged as he expected — Claude, OpenAI, Meta and Grok interpret the same prompt significantly differently — and pointedly notes that the open-source models are all very Claude-like in behavior.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Non-convergence means models are not commodities, preserving switching costs and provider pricing power — and the Claude-likeness doubles as his distillation evidence.
insights.quote: I will say if the open source models are all very cloudlike in their behavior. I wonder why.

insights.claim: Every major new model release forces Lindy to spend roughly $10,000 running its homegrown Pareto-frontier prompt-optimization loop over more than a thousand evals, and Crivello says the prompts change substantially each time.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Puts a concrete price on model-migration friction; automated prompt optimization is becoming mandatory infrastructure, an underbuilt tooling category.
insights.quote: it's like about like $10,000 every time like a new major model comes out

insights.claim: Crivello says most companies should not fine-tune — it is a last resort after every other option, viable mainly for at-scale companies that have exhausted the low-hanging fruit — though he expects it in Lindy Teammate eventually and notes current models can now largely do the fine-tuning work for you.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Bearish read-through for fine-tuning-as-a-product businesses, consistent with OpenAI retiring its fine-tuning offering.
insights.quote: Most people should not fine tune.

insights.claim: Lindy's error rate dropped 8x within the first week of putting its self-improvement loop online roughly two months ago, which Crivello says became possible only because post-GPT-4 models are capable enough to close the loop.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: An 8x reliability gain in one week from software scaffolding rather than a model upgrade suggests agent reliability is now scaffold-limited, not model-limited.
insights.quote: It went down by 8x the error rate.

insights.claim: Crivello calls an LLM-as-judge validator the lowest-hanging fruit in agent reliability: even naively asking the agent 'are you sure' before an action produces a measurable eval bump, and a 10,000-token checklist-style validator prompt can push performance above Opus level in Lindy's experience.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Cheap scaffolding can substitute for a more expensive model tier — a direct margin lever and a reason model-tier choice matters less than assumed.
insights.quote: literally if it's just are you sure already you get a bump on your valves which is insane

insights.claim: Crivello says Claude models this year have been getting dates wrong by one day, so Lindy prompts the agent to always write a weekday alongside the date and runs a regex-based deterministic validator, with no AI in the loop, to catch mismatches.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A named frontier-model defect with a cheap deterministic fix — evidence that symbolic guardrails remain necessary in production agents.
insights.quote: cloud models this year have been getting dates wrong by one day

themes.theme: Buy-vs-build and the agent infrastructure stack

insights.claim: Crivello has become strongly buy-over-build on infrastructure, explicitly countering the prevailing narrative that SaaS is dying because everything can be vibe-coded — he says infrastructure cannot be, because there is far more depth in those systems than founders appreciate.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A direct rebuttal to the AI-kills-SaaS thesis, scoped narrowly to infrastructure — supports continued investment in agent-infra startups while conceding the app layer is more replicable.
insights.quote: anytime I have an opportunity to buy instead of build, I will do it

insights.claim: Crivello's named production vendor stack is Mesa for an agent-native git-backed file system, E2B for sandboxes and Browserbase for browser management, and he strongly recommends decoupling the file system from the sandbox at scale rather than reusing the sandbox's own file system.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A production reference architecture from a scaled agent company — direct commercial validation for these specific private infrastructure companies.

insights.claim: Observability and evals are Crivello's stated exception to buy-over-build: Lindy evaluated LangSmith and Braintrust among others but kept the homegrown platform it was forced to build when it started in 2022 before agent tooling existed, now staffed by one full-time engineer and at feature parity or better.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Early agent companies carry sticky homegrown eval stacks, capping the addressable market for eval and observability vendors among the most sophisticated buyers.
insights.quote: I don't recommend doing it at home honestly

insights.claim: Because Lindy needs Slack admin rights to install, product-led growth works up to roughly 50-100 seats and then requires internal champions and IT review — which Crivello cites as the reason PLG taps out as you move up-market, despite Lindy holding SOC 2, HIPAA and GDPR compliance.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Defines the seat count where agent startups must convert from PLG to enterprise sales — a structural go-to-market inflection to model in revenue forecasts.
insights.quote: that's one reason why PLG eventually you tap out of it as you go up market

themes.theme: AI-native org design and the centaur era

insights.claim: Crivello has changed his mind toward consolidating as much internal work as possible under a single agent, arguing humans over-build multi-agent systems by anthropomorphizing — division of labor exists because humans have 24 hours and bounded context, constraints agents do not share.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Cuts against the multi-agent orchestration narrative many startups sell; the remaining valid reason for multi-agent separation is security, not specialization.
insights.quote: I find that division of labor is not a good reason to have multiple agents

insights.claim: Lindy's headcount has been flat while productivity roughly tripled over a couple of months, with PRs per week tripling and lines per PR also tripling, and the team no longer reviewing PRs so much as reviewing the machine that reviews the PRs.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Concrete internal metrics for the flat-headcount, rising-output pattern; if generalizable it compresses software hiring demand while inflating CI and compute spend.
insights.quote: we're no longer PR review wheels. were like PR reviewer reviewers

insights.claim: After two weeks of engineers failing to control an insulting CI bill across many hundreds of runners moved from GitHub to GCP, Lindy handed the problem to its own AI employee, which now analyzes runners and actions autonomously and sends a daily generated graph showing CI cost and time-to-merge falling.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A working example of an agent autonomously optimizing production infrastructure — the clearest near-term ROI case for the AI-employee category.
insights.quote: I can't believe it took us two weeks of just like messing with CI ourselves instead of just sending this to Lindy

insights.claim: Lindy's internal inference spend is now within striking range of payroll — payroll is still larger, but Crivello expects the two lines to cross in three to six months.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A dated, checkable marker for when compute overtakes labor as the dominant cost of a software company — the cleanest single metric for the AI-labor substitution thesis.
insights.quote: payroll is still greater but the lines are going to cross 3 to six months from now

insights.claim: Crivello rejects the centaur myth as a fantasy: he says the literature on chess and other games shows AI plus human first beats AI, then the gap shrinks and turns negative, with humans eventually adding at best random noise — so the current centaur phase at Lindy is real but temporary.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Directly attacks the AI-augments-rather-than-replaces consensus underpinning labor-market optimism; the investable question becomes how long the centaur phase lasts.
insights.quote: little by little the gap of AI plus human versus AI is shrinking until it actually turns negative and humans are introducing at best like random noise into the system

insights.claim: Crivello describes current frontier models as ASI in many respects yet subhuman in surprising ways — capable of one-shotting 50,000 lines of code yet deciding dozens of times a day to walk to the car wash — and says the industry has lost the vocabulary, including task-length horizons, to describe where agents actually fail.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Spikiness, not average capability, is the operative deployment risk metric — and it explains why headline benchmark gains have not translated into economic disruption.
insights.quote: Imagine you've got this this this machine that runs a company super smart but but but 50 times a day it decides to walk to the car wash

insights.claim: Both speakers concede they expected far more economic disruption and higher unemployment by now, with Crivello attributing the lag to model spikiness — however expensive humans are, they earn their keep plugging holes that are genuinely harmful to the system.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello and Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: Gives a mechanistic explanation for the AI productivity-paradox gap and a leading indicator: labor displacement should accelerate as spikiness falls, not as benchmarks rise.
insights.quote: as long as the models are spiky, we are going to need a lot of humans in the room because the holes in the model are very dangerous

insights.claim: Crivello argues incumbents stay disadvantaged as long as models are spiky, and that even a hole-free drop-in remote worker would be adopted skeuomorphically by incumbents — putting AGI into human-shaped seats and missing the organizational innovation smaller companies will find.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Argues the disruption window stays open for startups even after capability parity — value accrues to those who redesign the org, not those who automate existing roles.

insights.claim: Crivello invokes his 2018 tough tomato principle blog post — that each technological revolution is first described in the old paradigm's terms, as with horseless carriages — and says the term AI employee is itself a strong sign you are thinking about your product wrong, even if it is necessary for market positioning.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A lens for separating skeuomorphic agent products from natively designed ones — the outsized returns go to whoever discovers the medium-native form first.
insights.quote: AI employee is a strong as as a term is a very strong sign that you're doing something very wrong in how you're thinking about your product

themes.theme: Chinese model ban, AI risk and policy

insights.claim: Crivello states flatly that as of late July 2026 we have AGI, are in takeoff and have not figured out alignment, and calls the recent open face incident the most concerning he has seen — reporting that friends at the labs are panicking and that there is an air of intense fear.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A sitting AI CEO reporting panic inside frontier labs is a sentiment signal that could precede sharp safety-driven policy moves.
insights.quote: right now it's like July 2026 we have a GI we are in take off and we've not figured out that alignment

insights.claim: Crivello says he is in fervent support of a sweeping ban on Chinese models on US soil despite running his own company entirely on DeepSeek, framing himself as trapped in a coordination problem where he must adopt the models while competitors can.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A ban would strand the cost structure of agent companies now defaulting to Chinese weights — a tail policy risk to price into application-layer investments.
insights.quote: I am in fvent support of a sweeping ban of Chinese models on US soy

insights.claim: Crivello's position is explicitly not anti-open-source — he says he is undecided on whether open source raises existential risk and calls open source important for innovation including his own company — his objection is specifically to Chinese frontier models whether open or closed weight.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: The policy fault line being drawn is national origin, not licensing, implying US open-weight efforts could be spared while Chinese weights are targeted.
insights.quote: I have something against Chinese frontier models whether they're open or closed source

insights.claim: Crivello's first argument is unfair competition via distillation: he says Chinese labs are obviously distilling US models in violation of terms of service and possibly illegally circumventing anti-distillation measures, converting a billions-of-dollars training cost into hundreds of millions at most.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: If the distillation cost asymmetry is real, frontier training moats are far weaker than headline capex figures suggest.
insights.quote: if you do that training on human data it's costing you billions of dollars like actually billions of dollars. If you do it on on AI data it's costing you hundreds of millions at best

insights.claim: Crivello's second argument is propaganda plus agency: Chinese models are ultimately subject to CCP censorship — his own product refuses to discuss Tiananmen — and because they are agentic and doing real work in the economy, deploying them at scale would be the greatest instrument of foreign propaganda ever on American soil.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: He frames the precedent as the 20th-century radio acts and the TikTok ban, suggesting a plausible regulatory template and timeline for US action against Chinese weights.
insights.quote: this basically amounts to being the greatest instrument of foreign propaganda on American soil ever

insights.claim: Crivello argues that permitting distillation kills innovation on the same logic as patents and IP, saying that applying the pro-copying standard to pharma would produce very cheap drugs and no new drugs ever, and that people back open models because free stuff is visible while foregone innovation is not.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: The pharma analogy is the strongest available policy argument for treating model weights as protected IP — watch for it appearing in actual legislative language.
insights.quote: If you apply the same standard you're applying now to, for example, the pharma industry, you would have very cheap drugs, which is awesome. And you would have no new drug ever.

insights.claim: Labenz counters that Anthropic has no moral high ground on consent because Claude itself was built by hoovering up human knowledge including Chinese digitized heritage without consent, and argues it should not be the state's job to enforce a private company's anti-distillation terms of service.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: Captures the central rebuttal any US anti-distillation policy will face; its resolution shapes the legal status of model weights.
insights.quote: It's not like Anthropic has a super or any AI company has like a super moral high ground in terms of I didn't get my check for my share of the training data

insights.claim: Labenz proposes an insurance requirement instead of a ban — cheaper premiums for Claude-powered systems, higher for DeepSeek-powered ones — as a market mechanism that risk-adjusts total cost while preserving access to Chinese open weights, and Crivello says he would be down for it.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: An AI-liability insurance market is a plausible emergent category if this compromise gains traction — an underbuilt space with regulatory tailwind potential.
insights.quote: maybe you get a cheaper rate on your insurance. if it's powered by deepseek and we there's some unknowns like maybe you have a higher rate on your insurance

insights.claim: Crivello favors creating an FAA-equivalent agency for AI that would certify which models are acceptable, permitting sanitized or fine-tuned Chinese models, and argues no private company will fund such de-biasing work because it is a public good with no market demand.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: A named regulatory architecture from a builder; a certification agency would create compliance-cost moats favoring large incumbents over small agent startups.
insights.quote: I am in favor of like an FAA for for AI. I do think we need a new agency to regulate those models

insights.claim: Crivello concedes mechanistic interpretability has progressed but is unsolved, so a CCP backdoor triggered by a magic word cannot be ruled out, while Labenz argues sparse-autoencoder techniques from Anthropic research are increasingly able to find sleeper-agent-style behaviors reliably.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello and Nathan Labenz
insights.so_what: Interpretability maturity is the pivot variable determining whether Chinese weights get banned or merely audited — progress there directly weakens the ban's case.
insights.quote: there could be just like a back door of like you say the magic word to the model and all of a sudden it does whatever you want and only the CCP has this magic world

insights.claim: Crivello says he would not be surprised if laws eventually forbid AI labs from subsidizing tokens as aggressively as they do, because the price discrimination between API pricing and first-party subscriptions like Claude Max or GPT Pro makes it very hard for an application layer to emerge.
insights.speaker: Flo Crivello
insights.so_what: Names subsidized first-party subscriptions as a structural threat to the entire AI application layer, and flags antitrust-style intervention as a live tail scenario.
insights.quote: it's hard it's hard to compete against tokens that are as heavily subsidized as as what Labs are doing
